There are a number of specific requirements which apply when providing care within an acute hospital setting.

The service must support a real time Admission, Transfer and Discharge (ADT) process at ward level with the flexibility to support live bed management processes with user friendly functionality and reporting.

The service must ensure that all patient demographics are fed from the master patient / service user index (MP/SUI) to an appropriate in-patient module and the minimum data set for in-patient care is collected on admission, throughout the care process and completed on discharge. .
The service must support shared care including the automatic transfer of patients to new consultants, according to parameters such as specialty and location.

The service must support the latest versions of all ASTEMIA Medical Solutions approved coding classifications, with inter-translation, and any standard encoders. The coding function must permit the retrospective correction of incomplete episodes.

The service must be able to record and manipulate data pertinent to inpatient, day case and ward attender investigations and treatment, to encompass pre-admissions for elective patients, admissions, transfers between locations, specialties & consultants, discharges, clinical coding and bed management.
The service must link the administration of admitted patient care to the booking of clinical, theatre and lab resources. For example:
The service must provide for the specific requirements of maternity admissions involving the baby as well as the mother, the linking of the two, and the statutory notification documentation.

The service must provide for the communication (electronically and/or by paper) of pre-discharge, transfer and discharge information to medical doctors, community clinicians, patients and other relevant parties e.g. social services

The service must make available aggregate activity and individual patient based reports in as near "real time" as possible. There must be a facility to include data from all sources at departmental / specialty level

The service must assist in the planning of bed usage. For example, for routine/planned admissions an expected length of stay should automatically generate an expected discharge date which in turn can be used to provide a forecast of bed availability to be used when booking routine admissions.

The service must be capable of identifying the data on the clinical needs of current and prospective patients (e.g. clinical priority indicators and acceptable waiting times both for elective and emergency admissions, prospective discharge dates)
The service must describe how other factors important to effective planning (e.g. staff availability, theatre availability) can be brought into the facility.

The service must provide a “real time” bed management facility, both for routine use and for periods when there is a pressure for beds. This facility must cope with all routine occurrences such as temporary availability of beds due to the patient being temporarily off the ward and for beds blocked by patients medically fit for discharge or transfer to a lower dependency area who are awaiting for example social services accommodation, relative availability or transport.

The service must provide for automatic referrals to be undertaken based on trigger factors at assessment, e.g. automatic referral to speech and language therapy if the patient is described as having dysphasia.
The service must be capable of recording patient movements during an inpatient stay, e.g. visits to other departments.

The service must be able to present a graphical representation of groups of wards and types of beds within wards, with the ability to move beds within wards, patients between beds and to identify unoccupied beds, occupied and available beds.
The service must support “virtual bays” to enable admission to a holding bed
The service must be able to quickly display patient details, episode status and the status of any requested tests by, for example, ‘clicking’ on an appropriate bed icon
The service must be able to display historic bed-states, with identification of the type of each bed and its occupier, and enable ward contacts to be tracked.

Waiting list management is very important to the ASTEMIA Medical Solutions. Any ICRS service must have user-friendly reporting mechanisms to monitor and calculate Inpatient and Outpatient waiting times. Currently waiting lists are usually managed within Patient Administration Systems, sometimes with supporting manual systems. As current initiatives, including e-booking, are implemented, so the focus will be on provision of “access” rather than the management of waiting.

The facility is required to manage, document and analyse waiting times flexibly and at any one, or combination of, levels – for example by patient, by responsible health care professional, by department, by hospital, by site, by Commissioner, and by treatment.
The service must enable the tracking of user-defined groups of patients.

Conformance to both Patients Charter definitions of time waiting and statutory waiting list returns (KH series) with minimum impact on the user, and the facility to support any future Astemia  or local definition.
The management of guaranteed admission times should be automated, including a facility to review patients waiting according to user defined criteria,

The facility is required to link waits for out-patient and inpatient/day case treatment, and waits for e.g. diagnostic tests, to provide a total wait position, both at an operational, individual patient level and for subsequent corporate monitoring

A link is required into Trust wide resource scheduling services, particularly bed and theatre availability, in order to improve patient choice of dates and to lessen the likelihood of subsequent changes to admission dates due to non availability of resources.
The facility is required to produce operation specific information for patients at the time of adding to the waiting list and/or at notification of TCI date.
The facility is required to alert users of other events which may impact on wait time, for example if a patient on a waiting list presents for ante-natal clinic or is an emergency admission
The facility is required to calculate waiting times for outpatient appointments for new referrals by clinician and by specialty
Describe how communication with patients could be improved, for example by being able to quote average wait time by procedure/consultant/department.

The service needs to be able to identify whether the treatments for which a patient is waiting are connected (e.g. diagnostic test result required before decision to admit can be made) or unconnected (e.g. waiting in different specialities), in order to make more complete links to scheduling
Additional assistance would be welcomed in forecasting and modelling patients’ waits in order to improve planning of activity and resources

In order to produce optimum theatre lists there is interest in developing objective methods of assessing priority, incorporating waiting criteria and expected theatre time. Proposals would be welcomed.
The facility is required to hold common waiting lists by condition in addition to records by consultant.
The ability to suspend patients and adjust waiting times accordingly is required.
A cancellation must trigger the potential cancellation of all related orders and appointments, with a request for user confirmation of each cancelled event.
The service must support pending lists, linked to clinics and consultants.

The service must allow for the time consuming manual elements of clinic attendance management to be improved e.g. queue management. Scheduling must be flexible and there must be the functionality to allow other types of patient to be recorded, such as day hospital attendances, domiciliary visits, ambulatory, and nurse-led clinics.

The service should allow links with other functional requirements, for example to allow Booked Admission access from the desktop in outpatients or medical doctors premises. The service must also be flexible enough to meet the changing demands in terms of development of service provision.
The service must be integrated with or be an integral part of the wider resource scheduling and booking services.
The service must support flexible definitions of clinic sessions in accordance with the individual requirements and working practices of clinicians and departments.

The service must be capable of covering all outpatient activities such as non-consultant clinics, for example those of specialist nurses and CMHT’s as well as domiciliary visits, day care attenders and other patients seen outside a formal clinic setting.
The service must be capable of managing multi-disciplinary clinics, for example an orthopaedic clinic where an initial assessment may be made by a physiotherapist.

The service must be capable of supporting multi-task scheduling to cater for circumstances in which the patient requires tests or investigations prior to attendance at clinic. It must cater for combined appointments such that the patient need only attend the hospital once.

A totally flexible scheduling facility, involving minimal manual intervention, is required for rescheduling appointments. This facility must cater equally for re-scheduling individual patients and the block re-scheduling of clinics.

Maximum flexibility is required for a wide range of “priority definitions” to be managed and for searching for the most appropriate appointment, or series of appointments e.g. every Tuesday at 1500 hrs for ten weeks.
Facilities to record the outcome of each attendance /non-attendance and the actual clinician seen(non-attendance) must be provided.
The facility to clinically code all diagnoses and procedures undertaken in outpatients is required.

A facility is required to enable patients to be tracked during the course of their attendance both within and without the outpatients department in order that a patient’s progress can be monitored and enquires dealt with.
All facilities must be provided in such a way that all data can be recorded by clinicians at the point of care without unduly impinging upon clinicians’ time.
Once an appointment is allocated and confirmed a clinic letter must be automatically sent to the patient.

Following clinic attendance and on completion of a course of therapy a medical doctor letter must be automatically be generated and pre-populated with pertinent information from the ICRS and be ready for completion by clinicians
Individual care providers will require a casenote tracking facility within the ICRS service clinical information system, if the benefits of such a system can be proved.

Casenotes need to be available at short notice and their exact location needs to be identified. It is important that this module provides a friendly interface to everyone handling casenotes. Future requirements will include tracking of other documents and an ability to link to off-site storage areas is essential.

The move to electronic casenotes will require careful planning and support. In the meantime, it is envisaged that the use of the master patient / service user index and casenote tracking facilities will be required.

The service must provide a comprehensive facility to enable users to locate, track and request casenotes, both individually and as a batch when appropriate. Receipt of casenotes must be effected in a speedy manner.
The service must be capable of extending the tracking facility not only to casenotes but also to all other forms of patient record, for example departmental notes, X-ray film, ECG records.
The service must support the casenote retention policy, and to alert users to its contents and flag casenotes which should be retained/withdrawn.
The service enable users to record and view a complete audit trail for all transactions.
The service must automate casenote tracking for all patient movements.
The service must provide reporting facilities to highlight operational problems, both standard and user definable, are required.
The service must identify potential duplicate casenotes for the patient, including the facility to search patient details within the case note tracking module and update details.
The service must proactively facilitate the timely movement of casenotes, incorporating, for example, automatic reminders to pass on the casenotes.
The service must be able to extend the casenote tracking facility to any off-site location where records are stored or may be stored in the future.
The service must provide a method of reserving casenotes

Many acute Trusts operate a 24 hour Accident & Emergency Service which deals with urgent cases requiring medical or surgical treatment of members of the public. By the very nature of the service, i.e. dealing with unexpected cases or numbers of patients, an A&E department needs a reliable and efficient operational support services to manage these cases.

The service will need to support the A&E patient flow process, helps ensure relevant information is presented to the doctor, helps compile medical doctor letters, helps with auditing A&E activity and support the delivery of patient care.
The service must provide a facility to register patients attending A&E.
The service must provide a detailed history of care covering all previous A&E attendances and all other episodes of outpatient, inpatient, diagnostic, and PAMS care.

The service must comply with Astemia  standards for the triage (prioritising) of patients through the department and reviews of these priorities as the numbers of patients waiting increases or as time goes by.
Clinical staff should be able to override allocated priorities based on their own judgement.

The service must hold user definable ‘care pathways’ or protocols that will assist the staff in the delivery of care and act as a tutorial to new staff. These care pathways and protocols must be intelligently invoked when certain presenting complaints are seen .
The service must record RTAs (Road Traffic Accidents), and support the collection of income from compensation recovery unit. Such records must be linked to follow-up treatment.
The service must provide a facility to receive pre-arrival information from mobile computer systems (i.e. ambulance data) including times, drugs administered, readings taken etc.
The service must maintain a time and date stamped audit trail of all steps in the progress of a patient through A&E.
The service must provide a facility to indicate “at risk” category of patients i.e. – a frequently attending child, overdose presenter.
The service must show waiting information and patient priorities based on allocated triage code and time elapsed since triage.
The service must be able to record accident data based on: type of accident, environment in which accident took place (home/work/school/etc.), location of accident.
The service must be able to allow the printing of a master document for this particular ‘episode of care’ to which professionals can manually add treatments & interventions.

The service must be able to print post treatment management plans or advice leaflets to patients or carers. These should be ‘offered’ by the ICRS service as a matter of routine and should indicate when and where the patient should re-attend if appropriate.
The service must provide facilities to support major incidents.

The future vision for ASTEMIA Medical Solutions pathology is that of a service designed around the patient’s needs, providing fast, high quality diagnosis and supporting good clinical practice and good patient outcomes.

For patients, effective modernisation of pathology services means getting their test results back when and where they need them. They can expect greater choice in how and where they are tested, through innovative models of service delivery such as Point of Care Testing (POCT), which can be done where the patient is – outside the laboratory, in the clinic, in the medical doctor’s surgery, in Accident and Emergency or at home. Modernised pathology services mean fewer unnecessary repeat tests, shorter stays in acute care, and fewer delays for treatment.

Modernising information technology and management is a key strategy in achieving better service quality and efficiency in pathology. Managed pathology networks need a more integrated approach to information management.

It is not the intention in this section to repeat the detailed requirements of a pathology information service. Instead, the aim is to highlight those aspects which characterise future developments to ensure that pathology is part of the mainstream modernisation of the ASTEMIA Medical Solutions.

While laboratory computing has been at the leading edge of health information systems development for the past three decades, the fragmentation of disciplines within pathology and the lack of systems investment during recent years has resulted in a patchwork of pathology systems across the ASTEMIA Medical Solutions. The new technologies and new ways of working within pathology mean that new and more integrated ways of managing information are needed.

Modern pathology information systems need to meet both the multi-disciplinary practice needs of all pathology providers and users within a service network and have the capacity to address the key business issues of managed pathology networks.

It is recognised that most Strategic Health Authorities will not have the resources to introduce major new services quickly. However, this should not be a barrier to tactical changes in information services deployment and management.
There is likely to be many further developments in automated testing, point-of-case testing and facilities for transferring information. These could support new models of care

Pathology services of the future will be managed across a network of sites, possibly at the level of a health economy. This will require support for specialist access to information and support for management activities, such as monitoring quality of service provision.
